## Context

Noé included the revised analysis I provided on August 28 in the manuscript.
Noé sent the revised manuscript on September 8 and asked me to check it for
consistency and correctness.

## Review

The documents largely reproduce my revised results correctly, but several
corrections are needed.

1. __Figure 3 shows the wrong analysis.__

   The embedded figure includes `vo2max` and shows the sensitivity-analysis
   rankings. However, the adjacent _Results_ paragraph describes the primary
   analysis, whose temperature predictors have a different ranking.

   __Suggested correction:__

   Use Figure 3 from the `without_vo2max` analysis. Delete "standardized to
   VO₂max" from its caption: the primary analysis excludes vO₂max. Moreover,
   adding it as a predictor is not "standardization".

2. __We incorrectly suggest that adding vO₂max left both models’
   classifications unchanged.__

   I am responsible for this ambiguity. Writing _Adding vO₂max as an ordinarily
   penalized predictor did not change the held-out classifications_ (line 572)
   without mentioning the RF model suggests that it applies to both models,
   which is not the case.

   __Suggested correction:__

   > Adding vO₂max as an ordinarily penalized predictor did not change the
   > LASSO held-out classifications, and the final LASSO assigned it a
   > coefficient of zero for all three classes. RF accuracy increased from
   > 0.966 to 0.983.

   Moreover, I suggest using the same wording in the cover letter (although
   the cover letter correctly mentions that including VO₂max in the RF model
   increased its accuracy).

3. __The Discussion retains limitations belonging to the discarded subsampling
   procedure.__

   The sentences beginning _For this exploratory study, the sampling strategy
   reduces…_ (line 759) and _In addition, potential dependence at the subject
   level…_ (line 761) conflict with the revised LOSO analysis and the cover
   letter’s explanation.

   __Suggested correction:__

   Replace those two sentences with:

   > Although all eligible visits were retained and validation and bootstrap
   > resampling were performed at participant level, using the same LOSO folds
   > for hyperparameter tuning and performance estimation may introduce
   > tuning-selection optimism.

   However, retain the existing small-sample and overfitting cautions.

4. __Table 4 contains three numerical inaccuracies.__

   These inaccuracies are rounding errors.

   | Entry                                       | Current |   Correct |
   | ------------------------------------------- | ------: | --------: |
   | Exertion log loss, LASSO: upper CI limit    |   0.176 | __0.175__ |
   | Temperature F1, both models: lower CI limit |   0.849 | __0.848__ |
   | Macro specificity, both models: estimate    |   0.983 | __0.982__ |

   The values are rounded to four decimal places in the HTML file, and an error
   can occur when they are rounded further to three decimal places:

   * Incorrect two-step rounding: 0.175497 → 0.1755 → 0.176
   * Correct rounding: 0.175497 → 0.175

5. __The predictor description incorrectly applies five-minute summaries to
   local sweat rate.__

   This is another error originating in my suggested text.

   In *Statistical analysis*, all 51 predictors are described as summaries of
   the final five minutes. The code instead uses 48 predictors from six
   continuously recorded signals, plus three sweat-rate predictors derived from
   sweat-rate pads.

   __Suggested correction:__

   Retain the description of five-minute summaries for CBT, HR, both HRV
   measures, close-body temperature and humidity, but remove local sweat rate
   from that list and add:

   > Local sweat-rate predictors were the Stress-phase rate and its changes
   > from acclimatization to Stress and Stress+Clothing, calculated from the
   > phase-level pad measurements.

6. __Placeholders for the LASSO tuning specification and package versions.__

   In the manuscript (line 306) and the cover letter, replace `[λ_min]` with
   `10^(-4)` and `[λ_max]` with `10^1`.

   In the cover letter, use the following versions:

   - R version: 4.6.1
   - randomForest: 4.7-1.2 (used to fit the RF model)
   - glmnet: 5.0 (used to fit the LASSO model)

7. __The Figure 3 legend is inconsistent with the revised importance
   results.__

   The paragraph beginning _An overview of the results…_ (line 502) says
   close-body microclimate measures were most discriminative for both
   environmental stressors and highlights HR and CBT under exertion. The
   revised rankings instead identify sweat rate for humidity and SDNN plus
   sweat-rate changes for exertion.

   __Suggested correction:__

   Replace those interpretive sentences with:

   > Close-body temperature measures ranked highest for temperature, local
   > sweat-rate measures for relative humidity, and mean SDNN during stress and
   > local sweat-rate changes for exertion.

8. __The cover letter’s data-handling response is truncated.__

   It ends with _so held-out observations never con_.

   __Suggested correction:__

   > so held-out observations never contributed to their own imputation values.

9. __The Nogueira reference remains unresolved in the manuscript.__

   _Statistical analysis_ contains `{Nogueira, 2017 #2196}` (line 315), and the
   reference list does not contain the corresponding paper.

   __Suggested correction:__

   Insert the reference in the bibliography: Nogueira, Sarah, Konstantinos
   Sechidis, and Gavin Brown. “On the Stability of Feature Selection
   Algorithms.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 18, no. 174 (2018): 1–54.


10. __The abstract overstates the model comparison.__

    _Indicating no predictive advantage_ (line 48) is stronger than _providing
    no evidence of a predictive advantage_ (what I wrote).

    __Suggested correction:__

    Change that phrase to:

    > providing no evidence of a predictive advantage for RF over LASSO

11. __Height in Table 1.__

    This is unrelated to my analysis, but an SD of 10.2 metres for height is
    not plausible. I assume that the intended SD is 10.2 centimetres.

    __Suggested correction:__

    Use the same unit for the mean and SD, either metres or centimetres.

## Code availability

I support sharing the analysis code, but it needs further preparation before
release. In particular, I need to establish which of Kelly’s scripts produced
the results included in the manuscript. This will take additional work, so the
code will not be ready to share immediately.

Please let me know whether you would like to share the code and, if possible,
the data. It would also help to clarify whether the code is intended to
document the analyses or to allow others to reproduce the reported results
automatically from the shared data, without additional manual steps. The
preparation required will depend on that intended use.
